title: io-uring-coroutine-runtime — C++20 io_uring Coroutine Runtime with a Buffer-Ownership Contract, Cross-Core MSG_RING Messaging and a RESP Key-Value Server Measured Against epoll, Asio and Valkey

workstreams.title: Thread-per-core io_uring coroutine runtime in which operations, not coroutines, own in-flight buffers
workstreams.summary: A C++20 coroutine runtime on io_uring (liburing 2.14, Linux 7.0 on one Intel Core i9-13900K) with one reactor per core. Its one rule: memory the kernel may read or write belongs to the operation, not to the coroutine that started it, until the kernel's last completion for that operation has been reaped. It covers heap, registered and provided buffers, zero-copy send, direct descriptors, descriptor passing, linked timeouts, cancellation, shutdown and cross-core messages over IORING_OP_MSG_RING or a shared-memory doorbell transport, plus a sealed-memfd snapshot IPC protocol. Checked by test suites under GCC and clang with ASan + UBSan and TSan, deliberate contract violations and libFuzzer.
bullets: Built a thread-per-core C++20 coroutine runtime on io_uring (liburing 2.14) in which each operation lives in a reactor-owned slot addressed by a generation-tagged user_data and keeps its buffers until its last expected CQE (result, linked timeout, zero-copy notification), so destroying a coroutine with I/O in flight cancels the operation without the kernel ever writing into freed or reused memory.

Covered registered buffers, provided buffer rings with multishot receive, SEND_ZC buffers held until the notification CQE, direct descriptors reserved while any operation names them and descriptors passed with SCM_RIGHTS, and ran a sealed-memfd snapshot IPC protocol through the same reactor.

Verified the contract with 10 test suites (156 cases) passing under GCC and clang, each plain, with ASan + UBSan and with TSan; 15 deliberate violations, such as releasing a buffer at the cancel acknowledgement, returning a zero-copy buffer at the first CQE or resuming a multi-core call at its first reply, each fail a named assertion, and 600 s of libFuzzer per target (512.8M executions on the IPC validator, 4.51M on the RESP parser, each input also checked against a reference parser and key table) found nothing.

Traced the cost of one-way posts to a DEFER_TASKRUN ring (188 ns per message, against 104 ns to a COOP_TASKRUN ring) to the Linux 7.0 MSG_RING path, where a SINGLE_ISSUER | DEFER_TASKRUN target cannot receive the CQE from the sender (a kernel allocation, task work on the target and an RCU-deferred free); batching cut the kernel work to 15.6 MSG_RINGs per 1,000 posts, and freeing each post node on its own core brought the batched flood from 165.2 to 54.1 ns per post.

Built a shared-memory doorbell transport for cross-core messages (one single-producer chain stack per (sender, target) pair of cores, MSG_RING only to a core that announced it is about to sleep, with a sequentially consistent announce/re-check handshake): a round trip between spinning cores took 294 ns against 908 ns over MSG_RING and a 4,000-round lost-wake-up stress test passed on every transport, but 32 concurrent callers were 4% slower even with both cores spinning (126.7 vs 121.6 ns per call) and calls to a sleeping receiver were 7–17% slower (3,033 vs 2,844 ns per round trip, 220 vs 188 ns per call with 32 callers) and at 2 server cores and pipeline depth 16 the server delivered 4.78 M GET/s over the doorbell against 5.24 M over MSG_RING, so it stayed an option under a rule fixed before measuring; in a later window on a later build it delivered 0.997 of MSG_RING's GET and 0.831 of its SET throughput there, and by median 1.193 and 1.115 times at 4 cores, higher in only 5 and 4 of 7 repetitions.

workstreams.title: RESP key-value server on the runtime, benchmarked against epoll, Asio and Valkey on a shared machine
workstreams.summary: A shared-nothing RESP key-value server built on the runtime, with epoll and Asio front ends over the same parser and shards, compared with each other and with Valkey 9.1.3 over loopback on one shared Intel Core i9-13900K at 1, 2 and 4 server cores. The harness records per run the server CPUs' clock and the time other work spent on those CPUs and their SMT siblings, rejects and repeats noisy 1-core closed-loop runs under a rule fixed in advance, and reports CPU per request with io_uring/epoll ratios paired by repetition. The current figures come from two sessions more than two hours apart (7 interleaved repetitions each) and two more from fresh clones; a gain is claimed only where it held in all four, and each loss with its range over the four.
bullets: Built a shared-nothing RESP key-value server on the runtime (multishot receive into provided buffers parsed in place, one batch per target core per read, graceful drain on SIGTERM) plus epoll and Asio front ends over the same parser and shards, and compared all three with Valkey 9.1.3 over loopback; Valkey needs 1.7 times (1 core) to 2.7–2.8 times (4 cores) the io_uring server's CPU per GET at pipeline depth 16.

Measured in two sessions more than two hours apart (7 interleaved repetitions each) and two more from fresh clones that at 1 server core and pipeline depth 1 the io_uring front end needs 3–8% less server CPU per GET than epoll (lower in 5–7 of 7 repetitions); in the two main sessions it served 348k / 343k GET/s against epoll's 329k / 320k (Valkey 296k).

Reported the losses next to the win: at pipeline depth 16, by median in all four sessions, the io_uring front end needs 3–8% more CPU per request than epoll for SET at 1 core, 7–11% more for SET at 2 cores and 5–12% more for GET and SET at 4 cores, and serves 3–7% (1 core) and 8–13% (2 cores) fewer SETs per second; a 2-core GET loss seen in two sessions (3% and 9%) did not repeat in two more, and an earlier single-session 11% throughput lead at 1 core and depth 1 shrank to 3–6% when repeated.

Made the benchmark hold up on a shared machine: every run records the server CPUs' clock and the time other work spent on those CPUs and their SMT siblings (/proc/stat), 1-core closed-loop runs above 5% interference are rejected and repeated under a rule fixed before the measured sessions, and a probe showed that a busy SMT sibling alone costs about 30% for both front ends.

Wrote the load generator (kvload) for both modes: a closed loop on valkey-benchmark's pipeline model (1 or 16 requests per connection), and an open loop at fixed rates in which every connection sends on its own schedule and latency runs from the scheduled send time, so a stalled server is charged for the whole stall (no coordinated omission); in the two main sessions the open-loop medians of the io_uring, epoll and Asio front ends agreed within 3 µs at every rate (up to 200k requests/s on 1 core and 400k on 2), and p99 and p99.9, which swung between repetitions of the same server, are listed without a ranking.

Counted where the 1-core saving comes from: with the multishot receive armed and replies submitted in the same io_uring_enter that waits, the server made 59 io_uring_enter calls per 1,000 requests at 2 cores and depth 1, against 60 epoll_wait calls plus one read and one send per request for epoll; batching kept cross-core MSG_RINGs at 5.5 per 1,000 requests at depth 16 against 124.7 unbatched.

workstreams.title: Profile-first optimization of the server's request path in two rounds, each change measured against the build it would replace
workstreams.summary: Two performance rounds on the runtime and key-value server. With perf blocked on the shared machine, callgrind gave user-space instructions per request by module and per-thread user and system ticks split the CPU time, so the costly code was found before anything changed. Each candidate was built from its own source tree and measured against the build it would replace in the same quiet window, interleaved, under decision rules committed before the run. The first round, against the original code, was rerun in two sessions an hour apart and in an independent check from fresh clones. The second, against the first round's build, was decided in three quiet windows and rerun in two final sessions more than two hours apart and in two more from fresh clones.
bullets: Cut the key-value server's CPU per request at pipeline depth 16 by 16–26% against the original code on 1, 2 and 4 server cores (lower in all but one repetition across two sessions and an independent rerun), after callgrind showed the RESP parser and the key-value engine, not the io_uring runtime, were most of the 1,551 instructions per GET.

Rewrote the hot path every front end shares: a one-pass parser for RESP count and length lines with the old parser as fallback (same errors, checked by a differential test and fuzzing against a reference copy), an open-addressing table with linear probing and backward-shift deletion in place of std::unordered_map, and one multiply-fold hash for core and slot; instructions per GET (2 cores, depth 16) fell from 1,551 to 1,153 and CPU per request at depth 16 to 0.72–0.85 of the original code's on both front ends.

Replaced a when_all over one coroutine per target core with reactor::call_all, one awaiter whose cross-core call slots share a join counter and, if the caller is destroyed, keep their message nodes until the replies arrive; at 4 cores allocator instructions per request fell from 199 to 61 and CPU per request to 0.92–0.93 of the build before it (7 of 7 repetitions).

Measured and dropped five candidates under rules fixed in advance, among them leaner slot bookkeeping (2.6% fewer instructions, too few to show in CPU time), replies written straight into the send buffer, a registered ring descriptor and a spin before sleeping that cost 23–37% of 2-core depth-16 throughput on both cross-core transports; each one's diff and numbers stay in the repo.

Traced the gap to epoll left after the first round to user-space bookkeeping, about 130 more instructions per request at 2 cores and 280 at 4 in operation slots, message nodes and coroutine resumptions, and dropped a 5–6% 1-core GET advantage at depth 16 seen in two sessions when the independent rerun showed a tie (paired ratio 1.02).

In a second round, measured against the first round's build, built cross-core call nodes inside their operation slots instead of on the heap, kept slots in fixed chunks of 64 with inline bookkeeping, and computed each key's hash once and carried it to the owning core: callgrind instructions per request at 4 cores fell 11% (1,397 to 1,242; epoll 1,093) and 6% at 2 cores, and CPU per request at 4 cores 3–5% in three decision windows (SET lower in only 4 of 7 repetitions in the third), 1–4% in the round's two final sessions (GET lower in only 4 of 7 repetitions in the second) and 4–12% in two independent sessions from fresh clones; at 1 and 2 cores no CPU-per-request difference met the rule in all four sessions.

Narrowed the gap to epoll at 4 cores, depth 16, from 11–18% more CPU per request for the first round's build to 5–12% by median across four sessions, as the extra user-space instructions per request fell from 129 to 86 at 2 cores and from 283 to 149 at 4; the remaining gap is user time (145–168 vs 121–135 ns per GET at 4 cores, system time the same), spent on the operation slots, resumptions and message nodes that keep the ownership contract.

Reported the second round's costs against the first round's build: at 2 cores, depth 16, it served 2–13% fewer GETs per second in three of four sessions and 0.3–7% fewer SETs by median in all four; and dropped an inline receive path that ran 17 fewer instructions per request but needed 4% more CPU per GET at 4 cores than the build without it.
